Cobb Salad
INGREDIENTS:

1) 4 cup chopped romaine lettuce
2) 2 cup Chicken breast that has been cooked and finely diced
3) 1 avocado, diced
4) 1 cup cherry tomatoes, halved
5) 4 hard-boiled eggs, sliced
6) 6 slices cooked bacon, crumbled
7) 1/2 cup crumbled blue cheese or feta cheese
8) 1/4 cup Finely diced chives or scallions
9) Caesar or balsamic vinaigrette dressing

INSTRUCTIONS:

1) Arrange the chopped romaine lettuce on a large serving platter or in asalad bowl.
2) Create rows or sections on the lettuce for each ingredient: diced chicken, diced avocado, cherry tomato halves, sliced hard-boiled eggs, crumbled bacon, cheese crumbles, and chopped chives or green onions.
3) Starting from one end, neatly place each ingredient in its designated row. This presentation style highlights the colors and textures of the ingredients.
4) Once all the ingredients are arranged, drizzle your choice of Caesar or balsamic vinaigrette dressing over the salad. Use a light hand to avoid overwhelming the flavors.
5) Serve the Cobb Salad as is, allowing diners to mix the ingredients asthey prefer or enjoy them separately.

Plan for a 15x15 Plot
Hello vegetable gardeners! I'm a new gardener, and I'm working on designing a fall garden. I decided to enlist ChatGPT to help. What do y'all think of it's response? Much appreciated!

>I said:  
Hello! I need help designing a garden. I have a 15ft by 15ft plot to work with. I am planting the following vegetables: Arugula, Bok Choy, Green Beans, Kale, Kohlrabi, Lettuce, Mustard Greens, Peas, Radishes, Swiss Chard, and Turnips. can you design a garden layout that works with these vegetables?

>ChatGPT said:

>Certainly! Designing a 15ft by 15ft garden plot to accommodate all these vegetables requires careful planning to ensure each plant has the right amount of space, sunlight, and companion planting considerations. Here's a suggested layout:

>Garden Layout Design

>Plot Size: 15ft x 15ft

>Planting Rows:

>North to South Orientation: This orientation will maximize sun exposure for all plants.

>Layout Sections:

>Arugula & Lettuce (Leafy Greens Section)

>Rows 1 & 2 (Northernmost Rows)

>Planting distance: 6 inches apart in rows, with 12 inches between rows.

>Reason: These are quick-growing and can be harvested early, allowing room for succession planting.

>Kale & Mustard Greens

>Rows 3 & 4

>Planting distance: 12-18 inches apart.

>Reason: Kale and Mustard Greens can grow larger, so they need more space.

>Kohlrabi & Turnips

>Rows 5 & 6

>Planting distance: 8-10 inches apart in rows, with 12-18 inches between rows.

>Reason: Both need space for root development.

>Swiss Chard & Bok Choy

>Rows 7 & 8

>Planting distance: 12 inches apart.

>Reason: These plants have similar growth patterns and requirements.

>Radishes (Interplanted with Peas)

>Rows 9 & 10

>Planting distance: Radishes can be planted 2-3 inches apart, Peas 6 inches apart in double rows with trellis support.

>Reason: Radishes grow quickly and can be harvested before peas mature.

>Green Beans

>Rows 11 & 12 (Southernmost Rows)

>Planting distance: 6 inches apart in double rows with support for climbing.

>Reason: Green beans need plenty of sun and support, and they will not shade out other plants if placed at the southern edge.

>Additional Tips:

>Companion Planting: The combination of these vegetables works well together. For example, peas fix nitrogen in the soil, benefiting leafy greens like lettuce and arugula.

>Succession Planting: After harvesting radishes and arugula, you can replant with another crop like more lettuce or herbs.

>Trellis: Place trellises on the southern edge for peas and green beans to maximize space and sun exposure.

From the description, it sounds like you are dealing with some sort of weed or other plants growing in your onion bed. It's important to properly identify the plant in order to determine if it is a weed or beneficial to your onion crop. You can do this by taking a close-up photo and either comparing it to images of plants on an online resource or asking the community in a subreddit dedicated to gardening or identifying plants (e.g. r/plantidentification). You can also take a sample of the plant (flower, leaf, stem, etc.) and take it to your local agricultural office or a gardening center to see if someone there can help you identify it. Once you know what type of plant you are dealing with, you can learn more about its effects on onions and how to manage it accordingly.

Deviled eggs without mayo
For those who do not like the taste or smell of mayonnaise, I will share with you the recipe for deviled eggs without mayo, which is one of the classic appetizers of the parties. 

**Orginally recipe is here :**[**Deviled eggs without mayo**](https://healtyanddeliciousfood.com/deviled-eggs-without-mayo/)

 

**INGREDIENTS**

. 6 large eggs

. 1 teaspoon yellow mustard

. 2 small sweet cucumbers (grated)

. 1/4 cup sour cream

. 1 teaspoon salt

. 1 teaspoon dill and other herbs to taste

**DIRECTIONS**

1. We boil the eggs for about 10 minutes and keep them in cold water so that they can be peeled easily.
2. We cut the peeled eggs lengthwise and separate the yolk.
3. In a separate bowl, mix the yolks, mustard, sour cream, grated gherkins, salt and herbs with a fork until we get a smooth mixture.
4. We pour the mixture into the beaten egg with the help of a spoon or a cream bag (I pierced the end of the freezer bag).
5. You can serve it cold with a pinch of paprika and herbs.

Chipotle vs Qdoba 
I had a Chipotle and Qdoba burrito this week. Please see my official review. I have always been Chipotle over Doba, but never a Doba hater. Read my updated review and let me know where you stand. 

Both chicken burritos 

Qdoba Review
Price: $10.50
The Doba burrito was loaded up so much that it actually ripped, but the staff quickly double-wrapped it, which was a nice touch. I really enjoyed the soft, hearty feel of the burrito, and it was definitely bigger than Chipotle’s. The double tortilla added extra substance (and calories), which is great if you’re really hungry. The guac and queso were both solid additions, and I loved the salsa roja, which had a nice kick. A bit of Chalula added the perfect amount of heat.

Chipotle Review
Price: $9.44 (keep in mind the same Qdoba burrito w guac and queso would’ve added about $5 here) 
Chipotle’s burrito didn’t rip, which was a plus, but it was also noticeably smaller than Doba’s. The flavors, however, were more refined—the corn, pico, chicken, and sour cream all tasted fresher and more vibrant. Unfortunately, they were out of the usual Chipotle Tabasco, which I typically enjoy for an extra burst of flavor.

Verdict
The price gap between Doba and Chipotle is narrowing, and if they ever become the same price, this might be a tougher call. Overall, even though Chipotle’s burrito was smaller, I found the flavor more enjoyable. The competition is definitely closer than it used to be, but for now, I’d still lean toward Chipotle for the overall taste experience.

​

Ingredients  
▢800 g cucumber  
▢3 tablespoon soy sauce  
▢1 tablespoon oyster sauce  
▢1 tablespoon sugar  
▢5 clove garlic (adjust it to your liking)  
▢3-5 fresh chilli (adjust it to your liking)  
▢1 tablespoon sesame oil  
▢2 tablespoon salt  
Instructions  
Preparing the Cucumbers: Cut the cucumbers into strips and remove the seed part.  
Marinating with Salt: Mix the salt with the cucumbers and let them marinate for one hour. Then wash the salt off the cucumbers and squeeze out any excess water.  
Flavorful Finish: Mix in sugar, soy sauce, oyster sauce, sesame oil, chilli, garlic and your pickled cucumbers are ready to eat. Store some in a container in the fridge for later enjoyment.

Caesar Salad Kit does NOT serve 3! 😤
So I'm watching my diet and have been weighing everything. 

Today I was measuring out my **100g of the Caesar Salad Kit** and when I did, I noticed there did not seem to be 2/3 of the package left. So I dumped out all the lettuce from the package into a salad bowl and weighed it. **It came out to EXACTLY 201g.** 

So if we do the simple math, we see this is incorrect.

And normally, **I'd take the time to contact Aldi** (or any other store/brand) to let them know of the discrepancy. But **the one thing Aldi does NOT do well is customer support**. 

If you leave a detailed message for them through the website, I absolutely guarantee you within an hour you will get a message that they tried to contact you but couldn't reach you, and to please call their phone number. ***Every single time.*** 

I understand that's how they keep their prices low, by **not dealing with pesky customer issues**, but that's the one thing Aldi does poorly. Even Amazon and Target do better than that.

**Check your Caesar Salad Kit weight and let me know if this is just a New Jersey thing.** 

And BTW, there are 2 Caesar Salad Kits that Aldi sells. This one is not my favorite. It has little crouton crumbs instead of whole croutons. I mean it's good, just not my fav.

Suggestions on smashed avo recipes?
I've sort of been teaching myself to cook by basically making the same stuff over and over, but tweaking it regularly and experimenting to see what happens. I've found it's really helping me develop "cooking instincts." While I can cook basic things I'm pretty new to implementing herbs and spices; I live at home and my mother finds me developing adult skills an inconvenience, so the only foods I've ever learned to cook are breakfast foods because that's the only time I can use the kitchen without upsetting her.

One of the dishes I've been making over and over is smashed avo with bacon on toast. I used to just have it plain but I read a cooking tip online that adding lemon to stuff can really level it up because of the acid. It doesn't always work, but it inspired me to just add an ingredient here or there and it's really made the dish a lot better.

The base: three slices of crispy bacon on toast, with half an avo on top.

The variations I've played with -- each is mixed into the avo:

- The nutty version: I mix the avo with LSA and flaxseed powder, and then sprinkle with crushed walnut. S&P to taste. (Tried with lemon; the lemon doesn't make it *worse* but doesn't make it that much better either.) It sounds weird but it's actually pretty nice.

- The acidic version: I add a teaspoon of sour cream, salt, a squeeze of lemon, and chopped up dill. (Lemon performs much better with this combination.) This was how I discovered I have cooking instincts now, because I hate dill but I just had the feeling it'd go well with it, and it did!

(I did another version of this last week without the dill and with a small amount of ginger puree... I didn't really taste the ginger but tbh I think I'm afraid to add more ginger to see what it REALLY does; I haven't really heard of people using ginger with avo.)

- The version I made today: did the sour cream and lemon again, but instead of dill I added a tablespoon of a spice mix especially formulated for guacamole. Maybe next time add coriander to make it more guacamoley? Or even just actual guac.

Reading the above, does anyone have any suggestions of stuff to throw in and experiment with?
